_about: Every Section 35 grant in Michigan's school aid budgets, 2015-16 (state FY2016) to 2026-27 (FY2027). Hand-entered from the acts and House Fiscal Agency summaries; tools/build_history.py checks every quote 'q' against the cited source file and fails if it isn't there or if the amount isn't in the quote. 'fy' is the state fiscal year (FY2016 = Oct. 1, 2015 - Sept. 30, 2016). 'amt' is the final amount for that year after any supplemental, cut or veto; 'orig' is the amount first enacted when it differs. 'pay' maps state-aid payment-report lines (sources/parsed) to the grant: [program-year, report code]. Prose fields are plain text with *bold* only.

groups.title: The early literacy initiative (Sections 35 and 35a)
groups.intro: Section 35a began in the 2015-16 budget as a package of early literacy programs built around Michigan's third-grade reading goal. Its pieces have changed almost every year; each is described below.

programs.name: Running the early literacy initiative
programs.summary: General-fund money for the Michigan Department of Education's costs of running the new Section 35a programs.
detail: Section 35 set the goal for everything in 35a: programs "to ensure children are reading at grade level by the end of grade 3," so that Michigan would be "in the top 10 most improved states in grade 4 reading proficiency by the 2019 National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP)" and in the top 10 overall by 2025. Its money paid the department's implementation costs; in 2015-16, $100,000 of it was set aside to evaluate the parent-education pilots.
The 2017-18 payment report shows $150,000 of it paid to Wexford-Missaukee ISD. The 2018-19 budget (2018 PA 265) repealed Section 35 and moved the goal language into Section 35a.

programs.name: Extra reading time for pupils who screen as behind
programs.summary: Troy's one regular Section 35 grant: money for extra reading instruction for young pupils whom screening shows need help, split among districts that qualified by their first-grade enrollment.
detail: Districts could add instructional time "before, during, and after regular school hours or as part of a year-round balanced school calendar" for pupils in grades K-3 identified by department-approved screening and diagnostic tools (pre-K to 3 by 2020-21, and pre-K to 5 from 2023-24). To qualify, a district had to show it ran a multi-tiered system of supports, used approved diagnostic tools, taught the five building blocks of reading (phonics, phonemic awareness, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension), and had trained its K-3 teachers to read the diagnostic data.

The money was divided by each qualifying district's full-time-equivalent first graders; HFA put the 2017-18 rate at $210 per first grader. From 2017-18 a district could spend up to 5% of its grant on teacher training and up to 5% on screening tools, which replaced the separate grants for those. The first year's amount was cut from $17.5 million to $13.6 million in June 2016. The 2025-26 budget ended the grant: "Eliminates $19.9 million SAF."
programs.troy: Troy received it every year from 2015-16 through 2024-25, $135,630 to $183,750 a year.

programs.name: Early literacy coaches at intermediate school districts
programs.summary: Grants to ISDs to employ early literacy coaches who help teachers of young readers. The largest line that recurs every year, from $3 million in 2015-16 to $52.5 million in 2026-27.
detail: Each ISD is funded for a base number of coaches, and the rest is divided by each ISD's share of the state's K-3 pupils who qualify for free or reduced-price lunch. In 2015-16 the grant was up to $37,500 per coach and an ISD had to match at least half the cost; by 2023-24 it was up to $125,000 per coach, with two coaches per ISD funded first. Coaches work with teachers of pre-K to grade 5 (K-3 at first).
Oakland Schools, Troy's ISD, has received a share every year; its payments are in the table.
programs.troy: Paid to ISDs, not to Troy. See Oakland Schools' amounts above.

In 2025-26 the $10 million was paid to Gogebic-Ontonagon ISD. For 2026-27 it rises to $75 million, $50 million of it from the educator fellowship public provider fund, for an ISD chosen by the department.

programs.name: Literacy Essentials training (Gogebic-Ontonagon ISD)
programs.summary: Money to the ISD with the fewest pupils in the state, Gogebic-Ontonagon ISD, to train teachers and principals statewide in the Essential Instructional Practices in Literacy, working with the Michigan Association of Intermediate School Administrators.
detail: The training uses the Essential Instructional Practices in Literacy written by the General Education Leadership Network (GELN). From 2020-21 the money also paid for regional lead literacy coaches and principals' literacy training, and from 2021-22 HFA describes it as literacy and math essentials. The governor's 2019 veto struck a separate $300,000 for principals' literacy training.

It began with $1 million added in December 2018 (2018 PA 586). It moved into Section 35m for 2025-26 ($4 million) and became its own Section 35o for 2026-27. The payment reports don't list the 2018-19 or 2019-20 money; from 2020-21 they show it paid to Gogebic-Ontonagon ISD.

programs.name: Orton-Gillingham dyslexia training
programs.summary: Grants to districts and ISDs to buy training from an eligible teacher-training program for children with dyslexia, which HFA calls Orton-Gillingham. The law has the department pay them first-come, first-served.
detail: In 2020-21 the law described a one-on-one tutoring program; from 2021-22, a teacher-training program. MDE reports that in 2024-25 it paid the $1 million straight to the two approved providers, $400,000 to the Michigan Dyslexia Institute and $600,000 to the Institute for Multi-Sensory Education, to train district and ISD educators.

The 2025-26 budget dropped it and repealed the section (2025 PA 15). It returns for 2026-27 as $1 million in grants to districts and ISDs; MDE says the application opens in NexSys in spring 2027, first-come, first-served. (In the 2019-20 budget, the letter 35d was a $500,000 social-emotional learning pilot, which the governor vetoed.)
programs.troy: Not paid through state aid, so these records don't show whether Troy staff were trained.

programs.name: High-quality literacy materials
programs.summary: Money for districts to buy reading curriculum, interventions or teacher training chosen from lists ranked by the state's Committee for Literacy Achievement.
detail: The committee grades literacy series, professional development and tools by their likelihood of raising pupils' reading outcomes. Districts apply for one item from the lists, and the department pays what it determines a district needs to put that item in place. MDE reports 561 districts applied for and received 2024-25 money, which was paid in 2025-26.

The 2025-26 line ($70 million) also carried $4 million for Literacy Essentials and $1.6 million for the MiMTSS Technical Assistance Center (paid to Clinton County RESA). For 2026-27 it is $50 million, with applications in December 2026.

programs.name: Innovative community libraries
programs.summary: Competitive grants to districts that had set up an innovative community library, alone or with an existing library.
detail: A qualifying library engages and connects readers, provides resources to build reading skills, and involves community volunteers and donations. The payment reports show 7 districts paid in 2021-22 and 10 in 2022-23, from $50,000 to $212,000.

programs.name: Literacy dashboard
programs.summary: No money. By March 1, 2027, the department, with MiLEAP and the state's education data center (CEPI), must publish and keep updating a literacy achievement and opportunity dashboard.
detail: It must show, among other things, the share of children with access to free, full-day pre-K, the share of pre-K-5 educators trained in the science of reading, the share of districts using a curriculum funded under Section 35m, and multiyear literacy results on state tests, including grade 3 M-STEP.

checks.q: By not later than March 1, 2027, the department, in collaboration with the department of lifelong education, advancement, and potential, and the center, shall publish
The percentage of pre-K to grade 5 educators in this state who are trained in the science of reading
The percentage of districts in this state using a curriculum funded under section 35m
